content: Alcohol consumption and misuse among young adults represent significant risk factors for both mortality and morbidity. Motivational interviewing (MI) is a widely utilized approach aimed at addressing excessive alcohol use in this population. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of MI interventions in preventing alcohol misuse and alcohol-related problems in young adults. To achieve this, evidence was gathered from multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and PsycINFO, covering studies published up to July 2015. Additional sources included clinical trial registries and references from systematic reviews and related studies. The review included randomized controlled trials involving young adults aged 25 years or younger. These trials compared MI interventions with no intervention, assessment-only approaches, or alternative interventions for the prevention of alcohol misuse and related problems. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were employed for data collection and analysis. A total of 84 trials, encompassing 22,872 participants, were included in the review. Of these, 70 studies focused on higher-risk individuals or settings. Studies with follow-up periods of at least four months were prioritized, as they provided more reliable insights into the sustainability of intervention effects and were less prone to short-term reporting or publication bias. The overall risk of bias assessment indicated that the evidence from these studies was of moderate to low quality. At follow-up periods of four months or longer, MI interventions demonstrated modest effects in reducing the quantity of alcohol consumed. Specifically, there was a standardized mean difference (SMD) of −0.11 (95% confidence interval [CI]: −0.15 to −0.06), corresponding to a reduction in weekly alcohol consumption from 13.7 drinks to 12.5 drinks. Similarly, there was a reduction in the frequency of alcohol consumption, with an SMD of −0.14 (95% CI: −0.21 to −0.07), equating to a decrease in drinking days from 2.74 days per week to 2.52 days per week. Peak blood alcohol concentration (BAC) also showed a slight reduction, with an SMD of −0.12 (95% CI: −0.20 to −0.05), translating to a decrease from 0.144% to 0.131%. These findings were supported by moderate-quality evidence. For alcohol-related problems, a marginal effect in favor of MI was observed, with an SMD of −0.08 (95% CI: −0.17 to 0.00), corresponding to a reduction in alcohol problem scale scores from 8.91 to 8.18. However, this evidence was of low quality. No significant effects were found for binge drinking (SMD −0.04, 95% CI: −0.09 to 0.02) or average BAC (SMD −0.05, 95% CI: −0.18 to 0.08), both supported by moderate-quality evidence. Regarding other alcohol-related behaviors, MI interventions did not demonstrate significant effects on drink-driving (SMD −0.13, 95% CI: −0.36 to 0.10) or other risky behaviors associated with alcohol use (SMD −0.15, 95% CI: −0.31 to 0.01). These findings were also based on moderate-quality evidence. Further analyses revealed no clear relationship between the duration of MI interventions (measured in minutes) and the observed effect sizes. Subgroup analyses did not identify significant differences in outcomes based on intervention type (assessment-only vs. alternative interventions), setting (university/college vs. other settings), or participant risk level (higher-risk vs. all/low-risk individuals). Additionally, none of the included studies reported any harms associated with MI interventions. In conclusion, the findings of this review suggest that MI interventions do not provide substantial or meaningful benefits in preventing alcohol use, misuse, or alcohol-related problems in young adults. While some statistically significant effects were observed, the effect sizes were small and unlikely to be of practical relevance for policy or clinical practice. Furthermore, the inconsistency of statistically significant effects across different measures of alcohol misuse, combined with the moderate to low quality of evidence, raises concerns about the reliability of these findings. Any observed effects may be influenced by biases inherent in the included studies.
